attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post. It is not a quotation of the NYT material around it.

semantics.note: The normalised wording matches the causal mechanism. It shortens 'would otherwise be isolated', but the counterfactual is still implied by 'get by'.

contract.note: The plain reading (concealed incompetence, passing workplace checks, worse shipped code) is the ordinary meaning of the sentence. It is demanding, but it is not stretched against the speaker.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own disclosure of a learning RCT (2026-01-29). It covers short-term mastery of a new library by mostly junior developers. It does not measure baseline incompetence, workplace screening or shipped-code defects.

reviews.rationale: The only item is a learning-quiz study, which the contract calls insufficient. Nothing in the packet links low baseline competence, passage through workplace checks via LLMs, and worse released code. Nothing contradicts the claim either. attribution.note: Zitron's own framing sentence, written before he quotes the NYT.

semantics.note: Both parts are kept: uncertainty about net effects, and the causal claim that extra code volume makes running companies harder.

contract.note: Reading part one as uncertainty about net effects is fair. Reading part two as a general operational burden is fair. The Q1 2026 window was chosen by the evaluator, not the speaker, but it is reasonable.

evidence.note: METR (Feb 2026, independent) says its productivity data is an unreliable signal. That supports the first part: net effects were unsettled. It also says developers are likely sped up more than before.

Harness vendor survey of 700 practitioners (Feb 2026). Frequent AI users report more deployment problems and manual rework. The link is associational and self-reported, and the survey does not isolate code volume as the cause.

reviews.rationale: Part one, that net effects were unclear, is supported by METR. Part two, that code volume caused burdens across companies, rests on one vendor survey that only shows association and does not identify causes. The contract requires both parts, so the packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own first-person sentence in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'I don't see' framing. The emphatic 'fuck have I looked' carries an implied claim that no real public examples exist beyond vague partnership announcements.

contract.note: Testing the implied public-evidence claim is an ordinary reading of 'have I looked'. Counting detailed deployment disclosures as more than vague announcements is fair. 'Integrations that actually matter' is subjective and cannot be scored.

evidence.note: Anthropic disclosure (2026-01-28) naming ServiceNow's internal Claude sales-coaching tool and a company-wide Claude Code rollout. It is promotional and not independently verified.
ServiceNow's own release (2026-01-28) describing its operational use of Claude, with data-integration details. It is a company disclosure about the same partnership.

reviews.rationale: In Q1 2026, a named business, ServiceNow, published concrete operational uses of Claude: a sales-coaching tool and a company-wide Claude Code rollout. Both are described with implementation detail, so they are not just a vague partnership. This meets the contract's contradiction condition, with the caveat that they are company disclosures. The 'integrations that matter' part is subjective and is not scored.
